title: The orphans' property
hook: give orphans their property and don't swap bad for good (4:2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of an-Nisa: all people from one soul, and the ties of the womb. Your line was from one soul. Did you call your mother, or pray for her? Day three hundred seventy-seven.

A father dies and leaves a flock of good sheep to his young son. An uncle will manage them, and keep the ledger, until the boy grows up. The uncle has a few sickly sheep of his own. Nobody's checking. He could swap a healthy one for a sick one, once, quietly. Or mix the two flocks together, and let the numbers blur. The second verse of an-Nisa sees that guardian, and that ledger, very clearly.
screen: `A GUARDIAN WITH A LEDGER.` → `A HEALTHY SHEEP FOR A SICK ONE.` → `NOBODY'S CHECKING.`

segments.voice: Surah 4, verse 2, says: give orphans their property. Don't exchange the good for the bad. Don't eat up their wealth by mixing it with your own; that is a great sin. Three precise warnings, aimed at exactly the tricks a guardian might use. Some commentators read these lines against Medina after Uhud, with its new orphans and widows, and the surah turns to them from its first lines. A few verses later, 4:6 gives a whole procedure. Test the orphans as they near the age of marriage. If you find sound judgment in them, rushd, hand their property over. Don't rush to spend it before they grow up. If the guardian is well off, he should take nothing for his work; if he's poor, he may take what is fair. And when you hand it over, call witnesses. Then 4:10 gives a stark picture: those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth are swallowing fire into their bellies. Why so much care? One reason is close to home. The Prophet ﷺ was himself an orphan. His father died before he was born, and his mother while he was still a small child. Surah 93 says to him, in Pickthall's words: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?" And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports him holding up two fingers, side by side, and saying that he and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this. The verse turns that warmth into accounting. Love the orphan, yes. And also keep the ledger straight, because theirs is theirs.
screen: `NO SWAPPING, NO MIXING` · `TEST FOR SOUND JUDGMENT, THEN HAND IT OVER` · `THE PROPHET WAS AN ORPHAN` · `TWO FINGERS, SIDE BY SIDE` · then, large: `GIVE ORPHANS THEIR PROPERTY.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of a child somewhere who has lost a parent: someone you know, a family in your community, or children you'll never meet. Hold them in mind for a moment without rushing to fix anything. If you pray, you can ask God to protect them. Then think of one concrete way to help: a sponsorship, a donation to an orphan charity, time with a child who needs an adult. Pick the one you'll actually do. The bell holds the time.
Yatim, an orphan. Theirs to receive in full, with no swapping, no mixing, handed over with witnesses, from 4:2 to 4:10. Today's word.
Your line: theirs is theirs. Today, support an orphan cause in one real way, and return anything you're holding that belongs to someone else. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims treat caring for orphans and guarding their wealth as a serious duty; orphan sponsorship is a widespread form of Muslim charity, and Islamic law sets rules for guardians managing a minor's property.

fork.setup: you're a guardian. the orphan is nearly grown. according to 4:6, when do you hand over the property?
options: only when you feel like it.
when they reach marriageable age and show sound judgment, with witnesses.
fork.reveal: test them, and when you find rushd, sound judgment, hand it over before witnesses.

trapdoor: what you thought: be kind to orphans.
what it means: be kind, and keep the books: no swapping, no mixing, hand it all over when they're ready.
what a scholar hears: the Medinan setting after Uhud; rushd as the legal test of maturity; and 4:10's image of swallowing fire.
